title: 2 Kings 2:1–12
context: The unit should be kept intact. “When the LORD was about to take Elijah up by a whirlwind into heaven,” Elijah goes with Elisha from Gilgal. Three times Elijah asks him to wait, because the LORD has sent him on, first as far as Bethel, then to Jericho, then to the Jordan. Three times Elisha answers, “As the LORD lives, and as your soul lives, I will not leave you.” At Bethel and at Jericho the sons of the prophets tell Elisha that the LORD will take away his master from over him today; he answers, “Yes, I know it. Hold your peace.” Fifty men of the sons of the prophets stand opposite them at a distance by the Jordan. Elijah rolls up his mantle, strikes the waters, and they are divided, so that both go over on dry ground. After the crossing, Elijah says, “Ask what I shall do for you, before I am taken from you.” Elisha asks, “Please let a double portion of your spirit be on me.” Elijah calls it a hard thing, and ties it to whether Elisha sees him when he is taken. As they walk and talk, a chariot of fire and horses of fire separate them, “and Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven.” Elisha sees it and cries, “My father, my father, the chariots of Israel and its horsemen!” He sees him no more, and he tears his own clothes in two pieces. Both traditions take the taking up of Elijah as shared ground, reported as the narrator gives it. The “double portion” is commonly read as the firstborn’s share and thus as a request to succeed Elijah, not necessarily as a claim to twice the power; that sense should be hedged, not declared the only one. The imagery should also be left as the verse assigns it: the chariot and horses of fire separate them, and Elijah goes up by a whirlwind. The two should not be flattened into one picture, and the scene should not be forced into a type of later events.

verses.text: When the LORD was about to take Elijah up by a whirlwind into heaven, Elijah went with Elisha from Gilgal.
verses.arminianNotes:
The narrator opens with the purpose of the chapter already in view: “When the LORD was about to take Elijah up by a whirlwind into heaven, Elijah went with Elisha from Gilgal.” The taking up is the LORD’s act, by a whirlwind, into heaven, and the journey begins at Gilgal.

Arminian readers hear a real setting out. The event is announced before it happens, and Elijah does not go alone; Elisha is already with him. Which Gilgal is meant is discussed and need not be fixed here.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the opening as the book’s own frame. The LORD is about to take Elijah up by a whirlwind into heaven, and the two set out from Gilgal.

Both traditions keep this announcement intact as shared ground. The whirlwind named here will be named again when the taking up occurs.

verses.text: Elijah said to Elisha, “Please wait here, for the LORD has sent me as far as Bethel.” Elisha said, “As the LORD lives, and as your soul lives, I will not leave you.” So they went down to Bethel.
verses.arminianNotes:
Elijah said to Elisha, “Please wait here, for the LORD has sent me as far as Bethel.” Elisha said, “As the LORD lives, and as your soul lives, I will not leave you.” So they went down to Bethel. The first of three refusals to part is spoken under oath.

Arminian readers hear a genuine request and a genuine refusal. Elijah tells him to wait; Elisha will not leave him, and they go down to Bethel together.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the oath form: “As the LORD lives, and as your soul lives, I will not leave you.” The journey continues because Elisha will not stay behind.

Both traditions take the verse as the first stage of a path the LORD has set, with Elisha choosing to remain at Elijah’s side.

verses.text: The sons of the prophets who were at Bethel came out to Elisha, and said to him, “Do you know that the LORD will take away your master from over you today?” He said, “Yes, I know it. Hold your peace.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The sons of the prophets who were at Bethel came out to Elisha and said, “Do you know that the LORD will take away your master from over you today?” He said, “Yes, I know it. Hold your peace.” The company already knows what the opening verse has told the reader; Elisha knows it too, and he tells them to be silent.

Arminian readers hear shared knowledge and a real charge to be still. Elisha does not deny what is coming; he will not have it talked over on the road.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise note that the word is already abroad among the sons of the prophets, and that Elisha’s answer is plain: “Yes, I know it. Hold your peace.”

Both traditions take the prophetic company as witnesses to the day, without turning them into a symbol beyond what the scene requires.

verses.text: Elijah said to him, “Elisha, please wait here, for the LORD has sent me to Jericho.” He said, “As the LORD lives, and as your soul lives, I will not leave you.” So they came to Jericho.
verses.arminianNotes:
Elijah said, “Elisha, please wait here, for the LORD has sent me to Jericho.” He said, “As the LORD lives, and as your soul lives, I will not leave you.” So they came to Jericho. The second stage repeats the pattern: a sending, a refusal to leave, a journey onward.

Arminian readers hear the same vow spoken again, now toward Jericho. Elisha’s will is unchanged; he will not be left behind at Bethel.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that the LORD’s sending continues, and that Elisha’s oath is repeated word for word.

Both traditions read the verse as the second movement of the same path, still intact, still without a type forced onto the towns.

verses.text: The sons of the prophets who were at Jericho came near to Elisha, and said to him, “Do you know that the LORD will take away your master from over you today?” He answered, “Yes, I know it. Hold your peace.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The sons of the prophets who were at Jericho came near and said the same thing: “Do you know that the LORD will take away your master from over you today?” He answered, “Yes, I know it. Hold your peace.” Jericho’s company knows what Bethel’s company knew.

Arminian readers hear the knowledge confirmed in a second place. Elisha’s answer does not change; he knows, and he tells them also to hold their peace.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the repetition as the narrator’s way of showing that the day is known, not as empty doubling.

Both traditions keep the exchange intact. The taking away is expected today, and Elisha will not discuss it with them.

verses.text: Elijah said to him, “Please wait here, for the LORD has sent me to the Jordan.” He said, “As the LORD lives, and as your soul lives, I will not leave you.” Then they both went on.
verses.arminianNotes:
Elijah said, “Please wait here, for the LORD has sent me to the Jordan.” He said, “As the LORD lives, and as your soul lives, I will not leave you.” Then they both went on. The third request is to stay behind while Elijah goes to the Jordan; Elisha’s third answer is the same oath.

Arminian readers hear the last refusal as freely given, like the first two. They both go on, because Elisha will not leave him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that the LORD’s sending now points to the Jordan, the place where the next sign will be given, and that Elisha’s vow still holds.

Both traditions take the verse as the last stage of the journey together, still on the way announced in verse 1.

verses.text: Fifty men of the sons of the prophets went and stood opposite them at a distance; and they both stood by the Jordan.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Fifty men of the sons of the prophets went and stood opposite them at a distance; and they both stood by the Jordan.” The company watches; the two stand at the river.

Arminian readers hear a real audience, near enough to see and far enough to stand opposite them. The fifty will appear again when the search is proposed later in the chapter.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise keep the distance in view. The sons of the prophets stand opposite them, and Elijah and Elisha stand by the Jordan.

Both traditions take the verse as the setting for the crossing, without pressing the number fifty into a symbol.

verses.text: Elijah took his mantle, and rolled it up, and struck the waters; and they were divided here and there, so that they both went over on dry ground.
verses.arminianNotes:
Elijah took his mantle, rolled it up, and struck the waters; “and they were divided here and there, so that they both went over on dry ground.” The river yields to the rolled mantle, and both cross.

Arminian readers hear a sign given in the path, not a private vision. The waters are divided, and they both go over on dry ground, as the narrator says.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the act and the result: the mantle strikes, the waters divide here and there, and the two go over on dry ground.

Both traditions describe the crossing as it is written. Comparisons with earlier crossings may be felt, but this verse should not be turned into a forced type.

verses.text: When they had gone over, Elijah said to Elisha, “Ask what I shall do for you, before I am taken from you.” Elisha said, “Please let a double portion of your spirit be on me.”
verses.arminianNotes:
When they had gone over, Elijah said, “Ask what I shall do for you, before I am taken from you.” Elisha said, “Please let a double portion of your spirit be on me.” The request is for a double portion of Elijah’s spirit, before the taking away named since verse 1.

Arminian readers hear a real petition. The phrase “a double portion of your spirit” is commonly taken as the firstborn’s share, a request to stand as Elijah’s heir in the prophetic work, not necessarily as a claim to twice the power. That reading should be hedged, not treated as the only possible sense.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also refuse to over-specify the wording. “Please let a double portion of your spirit be on me.” is what Elisha asks, and Elijah will call it a hard thing in the next verse.

Both traditions keep the request intact and leave its exact force cautiously stated, without a party contrast over prophetic authority.

verses.text: He said, “You have asked a hard thing. If you see me when I am taken from you, it will be so for you; but if not, it will not be so.”
verses.arminianNotes:
He said, “You have asked a hard thing. If you see me when I am taken from you, it will be so for you; but if not, it will not be so.” The hard request is not granted or refused in a word; it is tied to Elisha’s seeing the taking.

Arminian readers hear a real condition. Seeing Elijah when he is taken will mean the portion is his; if he does not see, it will not be so. The outcome is not yet told.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise keep both halves: a hard thing, and a condition, “If you see me when I am taken from you”.

Both traditions take the verse as the rule Elijah sets for what Elisha has asked, still inside the unit that will now show the taking itself.

verses.text: As they continued on and talked, behold, a chariot of fire and horses of fire separated them; and Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven.
verses.arminianNotes:
“As they continued on and talked, behold, a chariot of fire and horses of fire separated them; and Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven.” The two images stand side by side: the chariot and horses of fire separate the men, and Elijah goes up by a whirlwind into heaven, as verse 1 had said.

Arminian readers let both clauses stand. The fiery chariot and horses, and the whirlwind, should not be flattened into a single picture, and the taking up should not be forced into a type of later events.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the same assignment of roles in the sentence. The chariot of fire and horses of fire separate them; Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven.

Both traditions receive this as shared ground: the LORD takes Elijah up, as the chapter promised, and the wording of the scene is to be kept intact.

verses.text: Elisha saw it, and he cried, “My father, my father, the chariots of Israel and its horsemen!” He saw him no more. Then he took hold of his own clothes and tore them in two pieces.
verses.arminianNotes:
Elisha saw it, and he cried, “My father, my father, the chariots of Israel and its horsemen!” He saw him no more. Then he took hold of his own clothes and tore them in two pieces. The seeing promised in verse 10 is granted; the cry is grief and a name for what he has seen; the torn clothes mark the loss.

Arminian readers hear a real lament. “the chariots of Israel and its horsemen” may speak of the vision just shown, or of Elijah himself as Israel’s true strength, or of both; the phrase should be left with that range, not reduced to one official sense.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise keep the cry, the seeing no more, and the tearing of the clothes together. Elisha saw it; then he saw him no more.

Both traditions close the unit on that seeing and that grief, still on shared ground about the taking up, and without inventing a contrast over the prophet’s authority.
